chapter: Streetcar, Cab revival shows and trips abroad
title: Solving the offstage music problem and the lawsuit with George Avakian
summary: The band's side-stage music drowned the actors, so Barefield proposed broadcasting it from a dressing room using radio methods and light cues. He ran the music, and Avakian later sued over commissions and lost.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: All right. So we started picking tunes and putting the tunes together for this Streetcar Named Desire. Then with, you know, with Marlon Brando and Jessica Tandy and all. So we went into rehearsal, and the first thing, trouble was that we had to play off the stage. So, of course, we had Marlon --
an organist, you know, played the harpsichord. Only he played from the stage. Good friend of mine -- I can't think of his name right now. He died -- Marlon -- well, I'll think of it.

Anyway, so the trouble was we had to play off the side of the stage. This was a DRAMA drummer. And it was just incidental music. We did all the old jazz tunes like, oh, Tin Roof Blues and so on, et cetera, et cetera. And -- but the music was so loud coming from the side of the stage, that it -- they couldn't talk over on the stage. And there was no way to bring it down.
And so now I just came out of the radio station, so I said, just -- why don't you broadcast the music into the stage from a dressing room?' And they said, well --
It would sound like it's coming out of a little radio.

Yes. And then you could have a monitor on the stage to bring it up and down, fade it out, any kind of way you want. So this is what they did. And so the -- so I copied the whole idea from radio, says, 'Just when you want us to play, you hit a buzz, and we'll get up in position to play. You'll have electric light there. When the light goes on, we'll play, and when you want us to stop playing, you'll turn the light out.' And it worked perfectly.
So we went on to -- went to New Haven and went to -- was it New Haven? No, went to Boston and worked out. So

finally we went down to Philly, and something they wanted -- they called and said something was going, was -- some information you wanted about it, and I said that, said, 'well, we'll have to send for George.' I said, 'You don't have to send for George. George doesn't know as much about what we're doing as I do.' 1)

And so George came over, and I just said, well, you know, forget it. So anyway that -- so anyway we came -- I took over the thing like this, although Layman Engel got the credit for it. The musical director, I was the musical director, and I set up the whole thing. And we came back to New York and went into the Barrymore Theater. This was there -- was there two years.

And so George Avakian actually, he sued me and the group for royalties and, you know, for commissions. And I got a lawyer, and we went to court, and they just laughed it out of court because they knew that, you know, I'd been into this jazz for 50 some years, and here's a guy that's just, you know, coming into it from reading books. And -- and he had no -- didn't have any grounds to stand on as far as that is concerned, see, because they -- he actually took the show away from me in the beginning. I could have gotten some decent money for the band, you know.
